## Introduction

As new language models and agentic systems are released, the evaluation benchmarks designed to test them are being solved at an unprecedented rate. Rather than asking *if* a model can beat a specific test, the more relevant question in evaluating AI progress is *how fast* that test becomes obsolete. 

In this post, we step back to look at the lifecycle of 36 major cognitive benchmarks. By analyzing the gap between the best AI score on the day a benchmark was published and the current state-of-the-art score, we can visualize the velocity of machine learning advancements and identify which domains are resisting saturation.


## Imports
```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```


## 1.Data Source & Pre-processing

This analysis investigates the cognitive domains where AI exceeds human capabilities using the [AI Benchmarks vs Human Baselines](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kylefengkfeng209/ai-benchmarks-vs-human-baselines) Kaggle dataset.


```{r}
benchmarks <- read_csv("data/benchmarks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(benchmarks)
```

## 2. Feature Engineering

To visualize the growth accurately, we need to isolate benchmarks that have both a release score and a latest recorded score. We will filter for benchmarks using percentage-based metrics (`metric_unit == "percent"`) to ensure a consistent 0-100% scale on our axis, calculate the total point improvement, and use the `short_name` column to keep our chart labels readable.

```{r}
saturation_data <- benchmarks |>
  filter(
    metric_unit == "percent",
    !is.na(best_ai_at_release_pct), 
    !is.na(best_ai_latest_pct)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Convert whole numbers to decimals so scales::percent_format() works
    best_ai_at_release_pct = best_ai_at_release_pct / 100,
    best_ai_latest_pct = best_ai_latest_pct / 100,
    
    score_improvement = best_ai_latest_pct - best_ai_at_release_pct,
    is_saturated = ifelse(best_ai_latest_pct >= 0.90, "Saturated (>90%)", "Active")
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(score_improvement)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)
```


## 3. Visualization

A dumbbell plot is ideal for tracking start-to-finish metrics. We will use `geom_segment` to draw the progression line, capping the ends with points to represent the score on launch day (`best_ai_at_release_pct`) versus today (`best_ai_latest_pct`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-benchmark-saturation
#| fig-cap: "The progression of top AI scores from the day a benchmark was released to the latest recorded measurement."
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 9

ggplot(saturation_data) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = best_ai_at_release_pct, 
      xend = best_ai_latest_pct, 
      y = reorder(short_name, best_ai_latest_pct), 
      yend = short_name
    ),
    color = "gray70", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = best_ai_at_release_pct, y = short_name), 
    color = "#E66100", size = 4, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = best_ai_latest_pct, y = short_name, color = is_saturated), 
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Active" = "#5D3A9B", "Saturated (>90%)" = "#1E88E5")) +
  labs(
    title = "The Velocity of AI Benchmark Saturation",
    subtitle = "Tracking the jump from initial release score (orange) to the latest state-of-the-art",
    x = "AI Performance Score",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Current Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

```

## Conclusion

The visual jump from the orange release points to the current leading scores captures the sheer momentum of recent model iterations. Many benchmarks that launched with AI struggling to clear 30% or 40% have been rapidly compressed into the >90% saturation zone. However, a few domains remain highly resistant to this explosive growth, indicated by much shorter progression lines. Recognizing how quickly a test can go from an insurmountable challenge to a solved problem demonstrates why static evaluations are struggling to keep pace, forcing the industry to constantly invent harder reasoning tasks to find the ceiling of these capabilities.
